utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are two short preliminaries and if the parties would not mind, I'll introduce them myself. First, for the Prosecution. The English translation for P468 which was admitted through Dorothea Hanson on the 7th of November, last year, contains pages which do not reflect the B/C/S original, and the Chamber understands that the Prosecution has meanwhile uploaded a correct English translation under doc ID L010-5084. And the Chamber hereby grants leave to the Registry to replace the old English translation by the new corrected one. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, perhaps needless to say but you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we start, I just want to tender, and I informed the Prosecution this morning, 1D1462. I forgot to do that on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's the document that the witness had requested to take with him and so I just request that he be asked if he had any additional comments based on that review before it be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you -- it seems that you agree with the suggestion. If you do that, we'll deal with admission immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, you heard this exchange. Do you have anything to add, commenting on this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is maybe one issue that I would raise. In relation to page 4, there's a section that the JNA are writing about paramilitaries and giving an assessment on the strength of paramilitaries in this -- in this section. And they make mention of the SDA and the HDZ but they don't make any reference whatsoever to the SDS so the Serb organisations. I -- maybe that is some -- in my report, I make mention that there's a document not long after this which identifies that the JNA were providing weapons to volunteers and a linkage with the SDS as well. And it just seems slightly odd that if the JNA are talking about paramilitaries or all groups causing tensions that there's something of a demission on this page in dealing with the strength and organisation of the Serb paramilitaries that were clearly operating at this time. I do, however, accept that the -- much of the document is talking about trying to reduce ethnic tensions but that is an issue that I had mentioned in my report that the JNA were attempting to do that at the same time as very much converging with the Bosnian Serbs and in some cases providing weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you still want to tender it having heard the additional observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1D1462 will receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D415, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D415 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D1463 in e-court. I believe that we have this document only in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we can see that the Mesihat of the Islamic Association of Croatia and Slovenia receives money from the Arabic countries and uses it to furnish the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina with weapons. Did you come across this document in your work?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask the provenance of this document, sir? There's no B/C/S. It's just an English document here. But are you able to furnish me with some idea of where the document has come from and its background?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] This document come to us from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question would be where did the Prosecution get it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that it was one of the underlying materials for an expert report in a different case and we received it in that fashion. I can look into it in a little more detail during the course of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, whether this is the original version or not is still to be considered. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you ever come across this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even before the war broke out, purchased weapons?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't know. I -- I -- this was not a key fact of my expert report. I'm aware that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had some control over the Territorial Defence, the republican Territorial Defence, so it would seem quite likely that some, at least, TO weapons may have fallen into the control of the Bosnian government and potentially other methods, including purchasing weapons would have been open to them. But it wasn't [Realtime transcript read in error "was"] an area of my expert report, and I don't know the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the weapons were stored in mosques, i.e., Muslim places of worship?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which weapons, sir? The TO weapons or weapons -- other weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any weapons whatsoever. Did you know that? You have just given us two options. Now, did you have information that any of those weapons were stored in mosques?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't remember specific details on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In paragraph 2.5 of your report, and let me just ask the -- the Honourable Judges whether they have the hard copies of the gentleman's report, or would you perhaps want us to print new versions thereof? In paragraph 2.5, on page 61, as far as I can see, you say that the JNA was deployed in crisis areas such as Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Skender Vakuf. Would you agree with me that the units that are stated here, the 343 Motorised Brigade, and the 5th Kosara Brigade were deployed in Prijedor municipality? However, those units hailed from that municipality and people who were recruited into those units were actually natives of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the most part, they were. Not exclusively in the case of the 343rd Brigade, as I -- as I recall, but many people from those brigades were recruited. The brigades went to Western Slavonia and they were redeployed back there. Although in the case of the 6th Brigade, maybe not specifically referenced in this line or this paragraph, I know elements of that brigade did go and deploy into other municipality, such as Krupe and Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you put your question, may I deal with a matter of the record. On page 4, line 23, you can read there, "But it was an area of my expert report." But I understood the witness as having said "... it wasn't an area of my expert report." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 6th Partizan Brigade, is it correct that its members hailed from Sanski Most and that it was also redeployed into the area from which it was first deployed into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think on the whole. There were other officers of the brigade who I believe were not from Sanski Most, but the brigade hailed from that area. Then it went to Western Slavonia. It was redeployed there in the latter part of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, those units that were in Croatia were then redeployed into those territories from which they originally hailed. They were not redeployed there because those were crisis areas.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the 1st -- the 5th Corps referred to some of those areas as crisis areas. They didn't go back to those areas and draw down or disband or go back to their barracks and -- and go on leave. I know very quickly elements of the 43rd Brigade, when they were deployed to Prijedor, they were deployed to combat locations. So they weren't disbanded or -- or drawn down in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move on, I would like tender 1D1463 into evidence. This is the previous document that we saw detailing with the purchase of weapons by the Muslim association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd suggest it be marked for identification at this time, pending further provenance information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand from the document itself now that it is supposed to have been signed or confirmed by persons, and for that reason most likely this is not the original. And if it comes from an expert in another case, then it might be important to find out where that expert got it from. Since the witness cannot tell us anything about it, it would be marked for identification. The Chamber is not only interested in the provenance but also whether this is a document which should be bar tabled or whether it should come in through this witness because the witness couldn't tell us anything about it. Please proceed. You need a number for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1463 receives number D416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D416 is admitted -- is marked for identification. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at 1D1464.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it appears on the screen, we will see that the document was issued by the public security station in Prijedor, i.e., the Prijedor police, on the 18th of May, 1992. And the subject are paramilitary formations and their strength in the municipality of Prijedor. Did you include this document into your review? Did you have it at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I don't know if it is footnoted in my report. It's been some time now since I've seen these documents, and I don't know if I've included this one in the Prijedor report I wrote or whether it's footnoted in my Krajina report. I would have to check that. But it is a document that I believe I've seen before. I would have to check that though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you this? I'm asking you this because you told us that you did not try to establish a strength of Muslim units. That's why I'm asking you whether you were privy to those documents that dealt with that aspect. And, secondly, why didn't you try to establish the strength of Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't -- I don't believe I said I didn't try to establish the strength of Muslim units. What I said was that the -- a study of the -- in -- detailed study of the non-Serb forces was not the core component of this report but there were references in the Krajina documents that clearly indicated that elements were armed. I make that clear in my report. I do make mention of specific incidents in -- in the Krajina municipalities, including incidents that resulted in the deaths of VRS soldiers. I make that clear in the report too. This document does seem to give an indication of strengths in -- in that area at the time, but it doesn't go against my general conclusion that that strength is relatively limited. We're talking about platoon-size strength here, company-size strength which is relatively small numbers, certainly in comparison to the strength of the 5th Corps, and that these units are predominantly armed with small-arms and hunting rifles, as opposed to the type of weaponry that was available to the 5th Corps and 1st Krajina Corps. So I -- I did not study in detail aspects, all aspects, of the non-Serb strength and opposition. But where it was evident in the Krajina documents, I made that clear, and I made my own assertions that I did not think that the strength was in any way comparable to that of the 5th Corps/1st Krajina Corps. And where it was evident, it was relatively lightly armed and in relatively small strength. That's not to say that they did not conduct operations. They did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just get clarification. Am I right that from your question you're insinuating that the -- these paramilitaries are Muslim paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where from this document do we find that they are -- they are Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since it's coming from Serbian side on the 18th of April [sic] after the take-over of power in Prijedor. Obviously that -- Serbian units wouldn't be marked as paramilitary at that time by this side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The power was over -- overtaken on the 30th of April [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but why wouldn't Serbians describe their own paramilitaries as paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also you can see through the names of the villages that -- first Ljubija, Donja Ljubija is Muslim-Croat village. Rizvanovici, Hambarine, Biscani are Muslim villages, Carakovo is Muslim village, and Kozarac is Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we agree that you are making deductions? You don't have hard evidence to say these are Muslims. You are making deduction because I don't want to go into further arguments with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you think that I am making deductions, but I think it is obvious from the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you think you are making the obvious deductions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop it and let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's stop it and [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you want to add to the decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just two quick things, Your Honour. First at the previous page, page 9, line 20 and 21, Mr. Lukic was reported -- recorded, rather, to describe this document as dated the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... May. The power was taken on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you would like to have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe he just has, Mr. President. The second is simply that the document is in fact cited in the Krajina report at footnote 637, and that information is -- obviously it's available to the Defence as well as it is to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Lukic, the whole issue of not paying attention to it seems to be totally moot. Because if it is footnoted, then that information is supporting or underlying the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.7 of your report, you say forcible take-over of certain municipalities by the SDS; namely, Bosanska Krupa and Prijedor, amongst others. Did you establish when the Muslims started militarily organise themselves in those two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't look in detail at that. But by the relatively quick nature of the take-overs, it didn't seem that the non-Serb population were particularly well -- well armed or well-able to stop that take -- over, if that was their intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I move further, I would like to tender this footnoted document, 1D1464.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't have any objection, Your Honour. I believe it is also part of a document that we tendered on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is, then we don't need to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that Mr. Lukic maybe check P2869 which is what I believe it's included in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The relevant is page 4 of the English of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we see that document, page 4 of P2869, then we can clarify it? Indeed, it seems to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we looking at page 4 of the document or ... yes. Okay. Then there's no need to tender it, Mr. Lukic. I take it, you would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw my proposal then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you take into account in that the conflict in Bosanska Krupa broke out because three Serbian young men were seriously wounded in Arapusa?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I -- I didn't take that into account into the specifics of that municipality. That may well have been the case. There were other incidents in Prijedor, for example, where there were flash-point incidents, I think, where individuals were attacked. But I didn't study Bosanska Krupa in that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of reference, in P413, which is an OTP exhibit -- perhaps we could show it on the screen briefly. 413. We need page 4 in English and we'll focus on what's at the end of this page, and in B/C/S we also need page 4, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are on page 3 in the English and not page 4, unless you are talking about e-court pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In e-court, yes. [In English] One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one second. [Interpretation] It begins on page 5 in the English version in e-court, but it's the fourth page of the document itself, and it continues onto the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The sentence that we need is the first full sentence on page 5 or, rather, the following page in the English version: "The incident in Arapusa, which occurred in the night" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please turn to the top of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see it on the screen: "The incident which occurred in Arapusa on the night of 19th/20th April when Muslim extremists seriously wounded three young Serbian men and the visit of Fikret Abdic to Bosanska Krupa, were the last harbingers of the war in this region."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you did not take this into account. So as this document has already been admitted, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it -- is it possible to read the previous page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Please just excuse me, I was told that you were to finish your testimony by Friday; is that correct? Or do you have some time next week as well?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have an appointment in Brussels on -- next week, but if I have to come back, I'm sure I can change that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was a kind of an agreement among the parties. This morning you spent [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to move faster. We cannot read all the documents here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you wasted quite some time on asking about a document which you said the witness would have ignored and then in -- of course, the witness would not know by heart -- with the assistance of the Prosecution it turned out that you had not properly studied the report and you had not looked at what the witness had presented. And then to blame the witness for seeking context, you should consider that you can't ask a witness to just focus on one or two lines and then say, Well, take it takes too much time if you want to see it in context. That's your -- let's not at this moment not further deal with the matter. We've heard what the witness said. But I'm urging you to use your time in a productive way in the interests of your case and your client. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Any other case where the witness wants to look at a document and Mr. Lukic would prefer to continue, we're happy to adopt the same approach we took Tuesday: Print the document so the witness can be provided with it by the usher and review it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the proposal, Mr. Traldi. I'll move on. Only I received information that the document is not exactly the same we proposed. And the Prosecution -- since their document has two pages and it's -- that document is from 14th of May and 18th of May and our document is only one of those from 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is two documents in one. The four pages, the latter part, that is page 4 is the same as page 2 in English. That gives the context and the background because it's all about the dispatch. Would you -- if you want to separate it, you're free to do so. If you want to leave it as it is then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will leave it as it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further on, in paragraph 2.75 of your report, you say that the Serbs used incidents of low intensity as a justification for mass attacks. You also say that the consequence of these attacks was the fact that 7.000 people were moved into prisoner camps. Did you analyse how many of the 7.000 people were civilians and how many were fighters?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I used the word "mass attacks" in that paragraph, sir, but I take your point. The Krajina Corps document - I know -- I believe there is one on the 1st of June - put of that 7.000, 5.000 in Trnopolje and 2.000 in Manjaca or Omarska, I believe. It may not necessarily be exactly clear but it would seem roughly that the 5.000 were civilians in Trnopolje and at least on that point they reference around 2.000 as fighters. However, many of the Manjaca camp documents -- or a number of the Manjaca camp documents make reference to the fact that during their processing they find that large numbers of those were not fighters but who were civilians who happened to be in the fields or houses in -- but rounded up and sent to camps nevertheless. So in specific numbers, no, the documents don't say exactly the totals. But it would seem that the overwhelming majority were not fighters and that that is known by the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are referring to paragraph 2.75 of the report. But I don't find any paragraph with that number in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I find it at paragraph -- page 87, but it doesn't seem to relate to what is being discussed. Maybe there is ... Is it page 87?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Eighty-seven. Page 87. And the paragraph is 275 [sic] I have cut it out here. And it's telling about 7.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We found it, and I think that's what you referred to. Let's always be clear 2.75 is not exactly the same as 275. That may cause come confusion. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have discussed Prijedor, the attack on Hambarine -- or, rather, in Hambarine, the attack in Kozarac, the counter-attack on Kozarac, the attack in Prijedor. Did you establish in your work that these were organised attacks which were part of a single plan, or do you believe them to be individual incidents, all of these?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the attacks by the VRS or are you talking about the attacks that the non-Serbs conducted on the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the non-Serbs who launched attacks against VRS members.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I argue that in the report that these are low-level incidents. For example, the attack on Hambarine was the attack on a check-point. The Kozarac attack was -- was on a travelling convoy, an ambush. The attack on Prijedor at the end of May was a slightly larger affair in that they tried to -- killed some soldiers on a bridge and tried to attack a hotel, which they set fire to, but they were overwhelmed very quickly. These were relatively low-level incidents, not necessarily something I saw as a widespread co-ordinated attack in that municipality or around municipalities in that area. There were -- there was an incident in Kljuc a little bit around that time. But, again, it was an attack on a convoy. And these were relatively low-level -- relatively low-level incidents. And the response was overwhelming and quick and resulted in thousands of people being taken from those municipalities. So if the question is: Do I think it was -- the attacks happened? Yes, they did. But my point is that they were small incidents. And around that time anyway, the Bosnian Serbs had taken control of those municipalities and were planning operations involving the police and the military to disarm units in those areas. So they happened within that context, not part of some planned, large-scale operation that I saw from the documents that the non-Serb population were conducting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of plans to join this part of Prijedor with Bihac, precisely by these military actions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And I wouldn't necessarily see attacking a check-point on a road or ambushing a convoy as indicative of a wider plan to secure territory that would link Bihac and Prijedor. I think it might take a little bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come across a list of members of Territorial Defence in Kozarac - I mean, the Muslims - who were around 3500 in their number while you were writing your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is a document I referenced in my Prijedor report, yes. And I think I discussed that there. Is this that handwritten list of individuals? It's some time since I've seen that document, and I think when I reviewed it many years ago that this seemed to be a proposal or a list of names of a localised structure that they were trying to establish. And that many of them had -- I'm -- if this is the right document, many of them had few weapons. So I do remember that document. But did I see 3.500 armed individuals in Prijedor when the attacks happened in late -- late May, no, I didn't. And I didn't see evidence, documentary evidence, of weapons seizures that would indicate that they had three and a half thousand armed men, nor did I see from the documents that the VRS forces that operated there can -- were -- were having to overcome a strength of that size and that -- the fact that they took control of the territory within days would seem indicative that that document was either a planning document or an intention that was not fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether the document was planned or not, do you remember that there were signatures in this document, signatures of people whose names have been typed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take it at face value that's what it was, sir. It's a long time since I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now we'll move to the Kljuc municipality. In your report, also on page 87, that we are already at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- document you are talking about, you didn't identify it. The witness apparently knew it. You put a useless question to the witness whether he came across that because he says, I referred to it in my report. You can't do that if you haven't come across. Then you didn't ask any question. The witness said -- assuming that that was the question that he gave the explanation, he says he has given in his report already, and there was something about signatures and there was no follow-up on that either. So there may be signatures. There may not be signatures. What that means -- it's totally unclear to us, so that's another couple of minutes wasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we saw that document before in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you tell the Court -- yes, if you think that every list of 3.000 that I would immediately know by heart what it is, then give a clear reference to what the report is and I'll look at that on my screen. If you don't put it on the screen, I'll do it myself for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we shall move on to the Kljuc municipality, also on this page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I have to deliver a decision and that is a decision which we would prefer not to delay. Therefore, I suggest that we take a break a little bit earlier. We would like to see you back in a little bit over 20 minute, Mr. Brown, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While he is exiting there was the one document he had asked to read. If the Defence -- it's the Krupe report. If the Defence has no objection, we'd provide it to the usher to give to him over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never have any objection for the witness to analyse any document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only to read. That takes too much time. No, I -- the Madam Registrar, you'll take care that once the usher has returned that he'll provide his services. Then I would like to deliver the Chamber's decision on the Defence notice, objection and motion, to bar Witness Treanor from testifying as an expert that was filed on the 25th of October, 2013. The Prosecution has not responded to this motion. It provided the Defence with the expert report through a notice of the 25th of September of this year. With regard to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber refers to its decision concerning Richard Butler, a decision which was filed on 19th of October, 2012. With regard to Treanor's expertise, the Defence submits that Treanor should be disqualified as an expert and the Prosecution should be barred from presenting his evidence. According to the Prosecution, Treanor was a senior search officer in the leadership research team of the Office of the Prosecutor. Treanor's work consisted primarily of collecting and analysing original documentary and published material relating to, inter alia, the Serbian Democratic Party, or the SDS, and the Bosnian Serb leadership. His work culminated in several expert reports which have been used in different cases before the Tribunal. The Prosecution submits that he will provide evidence on the political and military background of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia and the development of the Serbian leadership before, during, and after the war. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber is satisfied that Treanor is an expert who can assist the Chamber on matters related to the political and military background to the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and, in particular, the SDS and the Bosnian Serb leadership. As for any arguments related to the content and methodology of the Treanor report and about the impartially or independence of Treanor, the Chamber considers that such matters can and should be addressed during the examination of the witness. With regard to the Defence request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that he will be called to testify and the Defence will therefore have an opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides that Treanor may testify as an expert witness and denies the Defence request to bar the Prosecution from presenting his evidence. Finally, the Prosecution indicates that it only intends to rely on specific portions of Treanor's reports and it lists in its notice the relevant paragraphs. The Chamber understands that only the portions indicated are being tendered into evidence, and will confine its assessment of the admissibility of the reports to them. It also expects the parties' examination of the witness to be focussed on these portions. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, Mr. Lukic the Chamber has considered your question to the witness, whether he was available next week. The Chamber expects you to conclude your cross-examination tomorrow and that is based on our observing the way in which you conducted your cross-examination, relevance, time spent on matters without any follow-up. Many reasons. It's monitoring carefully your cross-examination which led us to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we left it off with paragraph 2.75 of your report. In the second half of that paragraph, you say in Kljuc, several incidents happened even before the attack on that municipality: The killing of a Serb policeman; an ambush on a bus that transported recruits through Sanski Most; seven Serbian soldiers arrested by members of the Muslim TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] and I would now like to call up D358. This document was issued by the public security station in Kljuc. It was issued in July 1992. We're interested in page 10 in the B/C/S version. The same information can be found on page 6 of the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will go quickly through the document. Under number 1 here, we can see that an ambush was set up in the Ramici sector. It is stated in here that the assistant commander of the police station in Kljuc, Dusan Stojkovic, was fatally wounded, and also that some other police officers were wounded. On the following page, in the English version, under bullet point 2, it says that a military convoy was attacked. The two soldiers were killed and a lorry driver as well. That six soldiers were seriously injured and 29 sustained slight injures. Of those who were wounded, four succumbed to their wounds. Under 3, we can see that an ambush was set up in the Tocina sector. Under 4, that the road between the villages of Velagici and Laniste was blown up. Under 5, we can see that there was an attack on the check-point in Velagici. It says here that a few days before that, on the 25th of May, 1992, and you will find that under bullet point 6, seven Serb soldiers were captured. My question to you, sir, is this: Do you consider this to be isolated incidents that had nothing to do with each other; or would you say that all those things were synchronised?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't say for sure that they were synchronised. They're obviously all taking -- occurring in and around the same areas which, I believe, are non-Serb villages. So I don't doubt these incidents occurred, and I make mention of them in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All of those things happened on the same day, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what would be your answer then? Were those things synchronised or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question that he doesn't know that it -- and he says it was on the same day. That's it, Mr. -- that's -- Unless the witness has any further knowledge. He says he doesn't have it. I take it that it's Defence's position that it was synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of those things happened far from the front line, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where was the front line, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of the front lines was in Croatia. And the other one is south, toward Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I -- I wouldn't necessarily agree that a front line in that classical sense. There was conflict, certainly, in other areas. Obviously there was convict going on in Croatia but there were -- and there was places like the corridor. At this time, it -- there wasn't -- it's not a classic war where there was necessarily very, very clearly defined front lines. There did come that time when territory was marked out. This is not taking place in classic front lines, but there were operations going on in and around this time in those municipalities. So it's a little bit less clear than maybe you -- you articulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report, you characterise all of those things as minor incidents. However, we can see that, as a result of those incidents, 50 Serbian soldiers became disabled in the course of just one day. According to you, what should happen to qualify something as more than just a minor incident?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't downplay that these incidents, you know, had an importance and that they -- that they occurred. My -- my contention is that certainly in relation to what happened as a result of these incidents and the operations that took place in and around that time on the municipalities when the response of the VRS was to take control of these areas incredibly quickly and to round up hundreds and thousands of individuals from those areas and to take them into detention. That's the contention. I'm not -- I don't argue that -- these certainly weren't minor incidents from the victims' perspective. And in Kljuc, in particular, there were a number of incidents and some of them related to Kljuc, some of them related to JNA soldiers that were coming from Knin, I believe, so I don't downplay the incidents, in particular. But in -- certainly they were relatively minor in -- in relation to the response and what happened later. You know, I don't downplay them. But they still were relatively small incidents with relatively small numbers of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what would then be your position? Was the VRS supposed to react; or was it supposed to sit and wait for further attacks and then react?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My argument is that many of these incident are occurring in and around already pre-planned operations to take control of territory. After the 12th of May, in particular, assembly session, there was a desire to control the territory that was deemed Serb. So, yes, there were these incidents, but they took place predominantly in non-Serb villages with that backdrop. Now, in relation to what should the VRS, at this time, it was the VRS, do or the JNA do, if they're attacked, clearly militaries have a right to respond to attacks and to take proportionate, legal measures in order to respond to those attacks, which could be to try and identify perpetrators which might be taking military action in that regard. Of course that's the rights of -- of -- of militaries if they're attacked. But bearing in mind this backdrop of a desire to control territory, the operations that were conducted in and around that time by the VRS, did not seem to be the sort of response, a measured proportion response, to this type of -- of activity. What happened was that within a day or so, or two days of this -- these incidents in May, large number, hundreds of individuals in Kljuc municipality -- well, firstly there were attacks on non-Serb villages, and hundreds of individuals from Kljuc municipality were taken into detention camps for which they were subsequently not released until many months later and sent as refugees. That, for me, does not seem to be a proportionate and measured response to this type of activity, if that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your response, which is quite elaborated, is based on the assumption that you analysed the military actions of Muslims and Croats and their strength. However, would you agree with me that in your analysis you did not deal with the military activities of the Muslim and Croat militaries at all?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the main focus of my -- of my -- of my report. The Krajina Corps archive documents did make some references to armed groups. They themselves were not incredibly detailed about the strengths and compositions of -- of armed groups in their own documents, and the fact that the VRS was able to use the weaponry that they had which, in essence, was JNA material, and to take over the -- these areas incredibly quickly leads me to the conclusion that whatever armed resistance or whatever armed groups were operating in these municipalities were not particularly strong and were not particularly well armed, certainly in relation to the weaponry of the VRS. But, no, I did not look in detail at every single issue relating to the military strength of the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, then, that for a proper assessment of a military on the ground, one should first start by assessing the strength of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, all I can say is that I lay out at the beginning of my report that there are limitations to the report. I put that at the beginning. This is a report based predominantly on the archives of the 1st Krajina Corps. It is not a report on every single aspect relating to the conflict in Bosnia, let alone every single aspect relating to the conflict in the Krajina. I used the materials as best I could. I think I might still be writing it if I had to look at every single aspect. But there are limitations, and I accept those, and I point those out at the beginning of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our suggestions is that your methodology is completely wrong, not that it is limited. That you studied the situation on the ground by studying just one side, completely ignoring the other. I would like to ask you this: Were you privy to the documentation issued by the BiH army while you were a member of the Prosecution team of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that other analysts were looking at other aspects in different parts of Bosnia and the conflict there, but I did not look at BiH material in relation to the writing of this report. It was formed predominantly on the basis of the Krajina archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the strength -- on the lack of strength of the Muslim side, did you come across the information that of the 65.000 members of the 1st Krajina Corps, 2.953 were killed and that 13.324 soldiers were wounded in combat with the Croatian and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in which period are you talking about, sir? Is this 1992 or is it through the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come across this information at all? And I'm referring specifically to the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that a large number of soldiers in the Krajina Corps were killed. The Krajina Corps was not just operating in the municipalities we've been talking about now, but they were on other parts of their -- their border. They suffered casualties, some casualties in operation corridor, for example, and the continuing operations to expand that corridor. They had casualties in operations against Jajce, in particular, and defending the border in Travnik, Bugojno, that sort of southern area, and they also launched operations, I believe, in the sort of Doboj Majevica hill area. So they were conducting military operations throughout the -- 1992, and they did suffer casualties, absolutely. They also suffered a very small number of casualties during these municipality operations but the bulk, I believe, were to do with these other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise for intervening. I've located the reference for the casualty numbers Mr. Lukic referred to that I think he has in mind. But if he has a reference for the 65.000 number, I -- I'd appreciate it, of the total strength of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, Mr. Lukic, could you also, by looking at the source for the 2.953, to tell us whether that is 1992 only or mainly 1992, whether we have any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That data --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I have for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on, that strength of this corps increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What's the -- Mr. -- the 65.000 are found where, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was my question. That's -- the 65.000 number is the number that I hadn't been able to find, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Comes from transcript I found in -- from the cross-examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not in evidence before us, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The evidence. We have 1D1474, that this data was presented to this witness, if you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, did the witness then confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I could not -- find that the document that this transcript is referring to, but I'm sure we will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what exactly is the source for 2.953? Where does the Chamber find that in the evidence; or is it not in evidence at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure we will provide that in the future. But if you want, we can see 1474. It's a transcript from Stanisic and Zupljanin. It's in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's 1474 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is the page number in Stanisic and Zupljanin. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sixty-seven is in e-court, page number. In e-court, 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The number of the document is 1D1474.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a Defence document. The last on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it has not been put on our screens yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet. If you want, we can put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have then D1474 in e-court. We need page 67, lines 9 -- 17, 18. This is the data I found. Obviously there was some document. It is mentioning the page 47 and there are losses per month. So -- but I was not able to locate the document by the number given in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- it's rather mysterious what I read there, but ... Would you put a question to the witness. Because, until now, I see the number appearing in a question rather than in -- in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, do you remember the cross-examination in the Stanisic case? Were you shown this particular document which supported the questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific document. It may well have been the combat analysis report. It may well have been the 1st Krajina Corps' own combat analysis report, I'm not sure. But I thought the strength of the corps was higher than that. But if this document articulates that 2.000, nearly 3.000 soldiers had been killed, then I take that at face value. As I explained before, I don't -- I don't deny that the corps was involved in operations, other operations in other areas for -- for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we cannot go any further at this moment. Your Honour, I would move on to the next area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let us discuss forceable transfer. In your report, under 1.43 and 1.44, you criticise the work of the Serbian members of parliament. We already discussed that and you have the minutes of that particular session. You singled out General Mladic's position as one of those who was against the transfer of the population. In your work, did you come across the fact that other peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina participated in the negotiations that resulted in the division of municipalities along the ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to go back to your point I single out Mladic's position as being against the transfer of population, I suggest that he warns, or I think in my phrase is articulates a note of caution about this issue of moving peoples and what it may mean for the leadership if -- if this becomes known. Now, the question you've asked is, did I come across the fact that other peoples in Bosnia participated in negotiations that resulted in the division of municipalities along ethnic lines. Can you -- are you asking whether I knew about what was going on in known Serb municipalities or in territories inside BH republic? Then the answer is it's not part of my report. I don't -- I don't know what was going on in those municipalities, but I do know that there were movements out in other areas of Serbs where they were vulnerable. But it wasn't a key area of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry if I was not clear. Do you know about negotiations done by Muslims and Croats in Krajina area with Serbs on division of municipalities? And have you found it in your work?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- the focus of my report was not about the political negotiations, per se. It was based on the military archives and the military documents. I am aware that -- that there were negotiations in certain municipalities about -- but it's not an area that I'm -- that I'm really across. It wasn't really the focus of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now I would like us to look at a document which is already an exhibit. It's P2366. Have you come across such documents while preparing your report, documents from Republika Srpska? And I would ask you to focus primarily on item 1 of this document ordering that the soldiers who have acted inhumanely, if they're prone to committing genocide against the population, should be sent away, also those who have a tendency to destroy and burn down buildings. And let us also look at item number 6, please. In B/C/S, it's on the following page. In this item, the brigade commanders are tasked with taking disciplinary and legal action. First of all, do you remember if you possessed this document at the time when you wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a document I recognise. I -- I don't know if I footnoted this in my report or not, but it's not a document that I specifically recognise. I do, however, make reference to a number of documents, other documents, of a similar nature which have been passed down by the -- the corps and, in fact, the Main Staff in and around this period about similar issues that they are to take measures against an array of offences, including some of the ones identified here. And those I have referenced in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even though you can see the English version on the screen, I would ask for your report to be shown on the screen; P2859, please. And we will need the extract in both languages. In English, we need page 97, moving on to page 98. And, in the B/C/S version, we need page 100. We are interested in paragraph 2.100. And let us read -- in the last sentence in the English version that we can see now. Then we'll move onto the text page: [In English] "The same report also noted that because Muslim extremists had failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village in Prnjavor municipality had been expelled." In B/C/S, we have to return to the previous page, paragraph -- yes. [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version, the word under quotation marks is, "moved out." In the English version, it reads, "expelled." In our view, there is a mistake in translation and, therefore, the conclusions cannot be the same. Therefore, we would like to call up the document that you are referring to here, and we need 65 ter 02837. It's a Prosecution document. And we're interested in item 2. That's where that text comes from. We can also see the difference here in the B/C/S version. I shall read it, the last paragraph in this section and it's also the last paragraph under item 2 in the English version. In the English language it says -- it's in the area in English and I shall read it in B/C/S: "In the Derventa sector there is still occasional artillery fire whereas in the Lisnja village sector, due to the fact that the Muslim extremists have not handed over their weapons, the Muslim population has been moved out." According to the original document, the population has been moved out. Would you accept that due to heavy fighting, it was normal to remove the civilian population, if that was possible?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say there was heavy fighting in Lisnja at that time in this report. No, I wouldn't say it's -- it's -- I wouldn't say it's normal or -- to move the population out. I -- this seems -- I -- I defer to the translation of expelled or moving out. I don't speak B/C/S so I was working off the translations. This seems to be similar to what happened in other municipalities: Deadlines to hand over weapons, either weapons not being handed over or not enough, or not handing them over, and operations which resulted in large numbers of non-Serbs being moved out or moving out of those areas after being taken under control by the VRS forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document now. It's 65 ter 08012; another Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the same time, you put to the witness heavy fighting. The document reads: There continues to be occasional artillery fire. Occasional artillery fire. Is it the position of the Defence that for that reason you have to move out the whole of the population? Is that the position taken by the Defence? Then it's clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our position is definitely. If there is fighting to start, army has a duty to remove civilian population, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which army, the attacking army or the defending army?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be [overlapping speakers]... should be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in the Defence's position is there any obligation to allow them to return to where they had been removed from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, that's clear. And you say occasionally artillery fire, as described here, would -- nevertheless would justify to take out the whole of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm asking for the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it is introduction for heavy fighting, occasional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say whenever there is a possibility of heavy fighting in the future, and we could ask the witness whether he has analysed what happened at this moment in time, whether the fighting was over or whether there was still a lot of fighting to be expected, but even then you already removed the whole of the population. And that's the position of the Defence. Okay. That's clear. Could you tell us what is described here as the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village having been removed, whether, on the basis of the military situation at that moment, that heavy fighting could be expected in the near future of that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would separate Derventa and Lisnja. So they're two different areas. So Lisnja is in Prnjavor municipality, I believe, and Derventa is elsewhere. So I think they're actually referring to shelling in one area then what's happening Prnjavor, in Lisnja, is -- even though they haven't written it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's -- then I stand corrected for misunderstanding what perhaps is not clearly written. In Lisnja village was there -- to your knowledge, was there any heavy fighting ongoing at the time when the population [Realtime transcript read in error "proposition"] was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to your knowledge. Was the military situation such that you could expect in the near future on from the moment when the population was removed that heavy fighting would break out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see in the document, sir, that the Krajina Corps was operating in a military -- in military operations in Prnjavor in that way. I -- I didn't see combat action at all. And I think this is related very much to the issue of the disarmament deadlines. But I -- to answer your question, I didn't see heavy fighting in Lisnja around this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from what you saw, was there any objective reason to expect, although it did not happen, that such heavy fighting would develop in the Lisnja area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything to give me that impression, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Lukic on page 37, line 19, in the question by Judge Orie, he said, "... ongoing at the time when the population was removed." What's written instead of "population" is "proposition." If that could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should slow down now and then as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time Derventa, which is the next town after Prnjavor was under Croatian control and that the line was in that area between Derventa and Prnjavor? I mean the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the confrontation line was close to Lisnja. But, yes, there was operations in the municipality of Derventa, which was part of that corridor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now let us look at the document which we have on the screen. We can see a document which is entitled: "Instructions." We have already mentioned the Arapusa village. So these are instructions for the evacuation of the population and refugees from the Arapusa local commune. And it reads: "Pursuant to the order by the War Staff Command of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa dated 29th of April, 1992, which orders evacuation of residents from the Arapusa local commune together with refugees from Bosanska Krupa, the Executive Committee of the Arapusa local commune has completed preparations for the evacuation of the population." And then the first bullet: "All residents of Arapusa and refugees from Bosanska Krupa, 460 people in total, will be evacuated." In B/C/S version, we need the following page, please. And in the English version, I'm going to read out the penultimate paragraph. It reads, I quote: "On the basis of the agreement with the War Staff Command of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa (with Mr. Miroslav Vjestica), as soon as peacetime conditions have been created, the command is obliged to ensure the safe return of the residents to their homes in Arapusa and the refugees to Bosanska Krupa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the position of the Defence that they were returned when peacetime conditions came?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The position is also if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was not to explain why it may not have happened. Judge Moloto asked whether it's the Defence's position that they returned. That's a simple question. Next question could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they did not return, why they did not return. That's the next question. Is it the position of the Defence that they did return?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know from this document that it's possible to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The question is what the Defence's position is. Because you introduced this document as an apparent indication of fulfilling or awareness and -- intention to fulfil obligations. Now, the question which was put by Judge Moloto was what they said they committed themselves to, whether that happened yes or no. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Defence has any position --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Might be relevant for the totality of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Green light, okay. You are aware that this paragraph says that the command is obliged to ensure the safe return of the -- of the residents. Now, is it the position of the -- the Defence that the command did comply with that obligation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not successfully it is not the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did it comply with the -- okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document, I will ask you this: In your work, did you see that there were War Staff Commands in the Serbian municipalities; and, if you did, what their role was in terms of commanding units.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't see them necessarily called War Staff Commands. There were a number of names: Crisis Staffs, crisis committees. Did I see the Crisis Staffs or War Staffs or crisis committees commanding units? No. There were one or two examples, I think. I think I quote certainly one example from Sanski Most, which would seem to imply some kind of order to the brigade. But, on the whole, I didn't see them commanding the VRS and units of the VRS. I saw them as a co-operative body which had military representation, yes; and there were decisions taken about security matters in those municipalities. But I didn't see them commanding the army, even though there were maybe one or two little examples that would seem to imply that. General Talic commanded his corps, and General Mladic commanded the 1st Krajina Corps. In relation to this document that -- if you want me to comment on this document, there are some echos with the previous document you asked me to review during the break. It makes specific reference to the Muslim villages - this is the document you asked me to review, that is - that they were, in essence, given an ultimatum that they could either stay and work -- operate under the Serbian authority or that they would leave, and I'm assuming this is a document that signed that agreement. Whether they had any desire to keep them there or whether they had that clause in just to say that they would have these individuals back, I don't know, but there were other areas referenced in the document you asked me to review during the break saying that Muslim villages that didn't agree were attacked militarily in Krupe. It is also of note that Miroslav Vjestica, who was a senior figure in Krupe and who is referenced in the document and also as a key player in the document you asked me to review, in which he is articulated as providing arms to the Serbs in the build-up in this municipality, he is also a delegate who speaks at the 16th Assembly Session. And he talks at that session about this issue of the removal or the movement out of the Muslim population from the right bank of the -- of the Una River, and he says in his speech there that will these people come back? And he said, With the happy news that the president has articulated the Una river as a border, no, they won't. And I might be paraphrasing it a little bit because I haven't looked at the exact quote. So there may be some context behind this. This document may be one that is being given as a document to the locals in this area to say, We will bring you back when the thing calms down. But his comments at the 16th Assembly Session gave you the impression that these people will not come back now that the president has articulated that the fourth strategic goal which is to have a border on the Una river for which this municipality is on the front line, that is that these people will not come back. I'm sorry, Your Honours, to be a little bit more long-winded in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08012 receives number D417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D417 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will briefly ask you whether you have seen that the presidents of Crisis Staffs, or as it reads here War Staff Commands, commanded Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one -- one other question. Battalion command, which is referred to in the document, which battalion do you consider that to be? Where Mr. Erceg I think is the battalion commander and a certain Mr. Jez seems to be -- play a role. Are these names familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are not. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to move to the paragraph of your report 2.134 which is on page 110 in English version, and 112 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're approximately at the time where we would take a break. So before we move to a new area --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Brown. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I forgot to tender a document into evidence. It's -- it is 65 ter 02837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02837 receives number D418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D418 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we said we would focus on your paragraph 2.135 and where you say somewhere in the middle of the paragraph: "In early May, the corps reported that people were afraid and that they were fleeing certain areas." The footnote is 520 for the document that we're going to see together now. This is 65 ter 09843. We can see that this document was issued by the command of the 5th Corps on the 6th of May, 1992. Would you agree with me that, on the following page -- or, rather, in English, we need page 2; and in the B/C/S version, we need page 3. This would be the last paragraph under 3. In the B/C/S version, it will be the first paragraph on top of the page. It says here: "People are afraid and panic-stricken. Many people are fleeing to other parts of the country." Would you agree with me that this document does not specify the ethnicity of those people who were panic-stricken. It applies across the board to all the people who resided in the area.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, sir, it doesn't make mention of the ethnicity. I would assess that it's most likely referring to the areas in the preceding lines. So, most likely the areas of Bugojno, Jajce Donji Vakuf and the Vlasic areas. So I would suspect that the emphasis is in those areas, and I believe at that time there was movement of individuals in -- in that area. I don't think it refers to the whole of the Krajina Corps -- well, the 5th Corps at this time, but the 5th Corps zone. Put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you come across the information, according to which, everybody was leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina or the area of Krajina to be more precise. Everybody: The Serb, the Muslims, the Croats.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe everybody was moving in the Krajina, all -- all nationalities and all peoples, no. Were there examples where Serbs were fleeing, yes, in some areas. But your question seems to imply that everybody was packing their bags and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it was not my intention to say that everybody was leaving because nobody would remain. The intention of my question was to ask you whether individuals belonging to all the three peoples were moving out of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I believe that you've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- one second, please. Of course, the most relevant question is whether people from the various ethnicity fled in an equal -- in equal numbers or in equal proportions from where they had been living.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see that, sir. What I saw was there were some references in that early part of May, like it's been referenced in this document, references to fleeing where it may not necessarily specify the ethnicity. What I saw later from late May into June and other months was that the overwhelming majority of the reports referenced Muslims and Croats leaving the Krajina. There were references in the Krajina documents to other parts of Bosnia where Serbs were fleeing. For example, I remember Jajce as being one area in May, where Serbs were leaving. That is a predominantly Croat, I believe, area. And there were references, again, I can't remember the specific ones, but references to Serbs in Central Bosnia leaving. But, in relation to the majority of the reports that reference the moving out of populations in the 1 Krajina Corps document, the majority refer to non-Serbs fleeing or being moved out or leaving the Krajina area, not Serbs leaving the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would add one exception which is the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last sentence says: "A few days after the beginning of war operations in Prijedor, Sanski Most, the 1st Corps reports that the population is afraid and concerned and the pressure to move out of the area is on the rise." However, before we leave this document, I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09843 receives number D419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D419 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your footnote 521, you refer to a document which we are going to see together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would to call up 65 ter 02836. It's a Prosecutor's document in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
