utterances.text: According to you, this is the cause why people are leaving. I'd like to see page 1 in both versions. And under 1, the second paragraph starts with the following words: "The Green Berets have been pushed back from the area of Jezero and Sipovo. The black shirts, too, have been deployed in the general area of Travnik where preparations are under way for an attack on Skender Vakuf. In the area of Vrhpolje, Sanski Most, the Green Berets have captured six of our soldiers. There is the highest degree of tensions present throughout the area and the expectations of a general uprising and assaults against all facilities and organs of authority." As a matter of fact, this implies that the Serb authorities were expected to come under attack; right? The date is 4 June 1992, mind you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document doesn't necessarily make it clear but -- but it says what it says that they are undoubtedly expecting attacks most possibly in those areas that they talk about, Travnik and other areas. I mean, the date of the document is important too. I mean, the date of the document is important too. I mean, this is 4th of June. Already places like Prijedor are under control of the VRS. Kljuc is too. Sanski Most is too. So to all intents and purposes, there was continuing mopping-up operations that were continuing in the weeks and months afterwards. But I think I quote this document in my reference because not necessarily for that issue, but that there is a direct reference that people are apprehensive and there's pressure to move out. Well, it's most likely that they were apprehensive because the municipalities that I've just mentioned are being taken over by the Serbs and that large numbers of people were now in detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time on the 4th of June, the 1st Krajina Corps, when they say that the authorities would come under attack, what do they have in mind? Do they imply the Serb authorities or -- or some other authorities? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it isn't made particularly explicitly clear in the document, but presumably they're referencing the previous lines in the areas that they're expecting the non-Serb armed opposition to attack. There were attacks in those areas. I don't deny that. But I don't use this document to -- to demonstrate that. What I demonstrate is a little bit later that there is this pressure and that people are fearful coming around the time that there has already been these attacks in the municipalities that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can also see under 3 that the document says that: "The crisis areas are Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor and Donji Vakuf and that they are under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps units. However, the population is fearful and apprehensive of the possibly escalation of new conflict, while the pressure to move out is increasing." In your work, did you find evidence that people left the area because they were apprehensive of new conflicts?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my report mentions a lot of phrases that are used in relation to -- to this. Some would be characterised in that -- in that manner. There's other issues about more forceful removals and pressure to have people moved in exchange for Serbs in other areas. So they use various terminologies and I referenced a few of those in this particular section. You might want to beg -- maybe the report begs the question about why people are being pressured to move out and why people are fearful. Well, maybe it's because of the activity that has been happening in the municipalities and -- in days or weeks before this report was written and activities which continued in areas after this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this is your interpretation of the document. In footnote 523, you make mention of two documents. Again, no specific reasons are given for the requests of the non-Serbian population to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before I proceed, I would like to tender the document that is currently on the screen into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02836 receives number D420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D420 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's focus on paragraph 2.137 in your report; page 112 in English and 114 in B/C/S. You refer to a document in the footnote 533, and in the document, it says that some Croats and Muslims are moving out and that the region of Bosnian Krajina has passed a decision that they should be allowed to move out on a condition that Serbs were allowed to move out from Central Bosnia and places with predominant Croat and Muslim populations. Do you remember that that was a condition that was set up to allow people to move out from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report says, that there -- these people will be allowed to go, as long as Serbs can come into Krajina territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this was done in order to make a relocation more difficult, not easier?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with you there, sir. This particular reference and other references like it seem to me to echo much of the discussion that was going on at the 16th Assembly Session. When you read the minutes of that discussion, the comments of Radovan Karadzic who talks about the issue of separation and separation of those who would be our enemies if they stayed in the same state, and the fact that he makes mention on at least three occasions in that speech about not having large numbers of people who could be regarded as against that state in RS territory, and the discussions, much of the discussions from the delegates which specifically make reference in some cases to this issue of resettlement of having Serbs in areas come to RS territory and non-Serbs moving out, this document is a reflection of very much the discussions that were going on at the 16th Assembly Session; namely, that the RS was going to have -- that the issue of resettlement was going to be a feature and that -- that large numbers of non-Serbs would no longer be present in that territory. This is a reflection of this issue of separation and the moving of individuals from territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just ask a question. The last question of this quotation that Mr. Lukic quoted to you says: "Those departing will not be allowed to return." What was the message in the 16th Session of the assembly in terms of people returning or not returning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read the minute, sir, that the emphasise was somehow to have this as a temporary solution to a conflict. And this document in -- as well gives me the impression that this was about ensuring that there was not going to be large numbers of people not -- who were viewed as being against the state within it and it was going to be a permanent feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You're telling us what was not -- what you didn't pick up from the minute and that it was not going to be temporary. Did you pick up that it was going to be permanent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the tenor of the whole debate was about two things, sir: It was about what is the footprint that we need to control; and the second one is, how can we ensure that we do not have large numbers of people who may be viewed as being against that state in it? And if that means relocation, so be it. And I did not get the feeling reading the 16th Assembly Session minutes that the tenor or language or thrust was about being a temporary solution that people were somehow going to be able to come back, and I think General Mladic's comments of caution would appear to also echo that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're discussing this continuity and temporariness, let us look at 1D1453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Lukic, I'm still puzzled by one of your previous questions where you asked: Would you agree with me that this was done in order to make a relocation more difficult, not easier. Is it -- do I have to understand that your suggestion is that they tried to keep them in by making relocation more difficult? Is that the underlying thought of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Underlying thought of this question was if there is another condition for leaving that it's harder to leave than without that condition. If you have the condition that somebody has to come instead of you, that's harder than if you can simply leave. That was my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- and that the intention behind was that to try to prevent people to leave, or - which is another option - that they firmly wanted to support that other people would come in and take the place of those who wanted to leave? That's another possible interpretation of that situation. But is it to keep them, make it more difficult so that they would not leave? Is that ... is that the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that having next documents in front of us would be more clear for everybody, and I think that the -- that standpoint changed over time but we will see, for example, through this document that is on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just puzzled by the thoughts underlying the question and we'll further look at the documents you bring to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have English version of this document? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about intentions and we drew conclusions about that. Let's see what's been put on paper. This is an order. It reads, "Serbian Republic Presidency." [In English] Just a second, since I skipped several pages ... [Interpretation] And signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Serbian Republic, which we can see on the following page. And let us see what item 3 says. Item 3 of this document dated the 19th August, 1992, reads, I quote: "Forcible resettlement and other illegal measures against the civilian population should be prevented, and any certificates of sale of property or statements that refugees will not return shall be considered as legally invalid and are declared null and void." Have you come across this document while preparing your work?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this order is completely opposite to your conclusions such as it is contained in paragraph 2.138 of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at face value it would seem to be the case, but there might be very much a contextual aspect to this. Could we go to the top of the document, please. This document seems to be written very much around the time after the international community has become significantly aware of the issue of the removal of people from -- well, the Krajina and other areas. It comes after the awareness in the international community of detention centres and the condition of detention centres, in particular, in the Krajina. And this may explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. This all your explanation which you are giving. But do you know whether people acted pursuant to this order issued by the president of the republic or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe they acted according to the document that he references beforehand in June. How this was acted upon after this time is -- is not something I'm aware of, but bearing in mind that certainly in the Krajina a large number of people had already left by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1453 receives number D421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the earlier period but after the assembly session which you mention, I would like to show you a document, 03022, a Prosecution document. We can see that these are conclusions from the meeting of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff. Under item 1, it reads, the first conclusion: "There are no reasons for the population of any ethnicity to move out of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." The date is the 20th of May. Have you come across this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure if I've seep this or not. This -- I believe this is a Kljuc document? From the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads Crisis Staff Banja Luka Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the end of the document we see Crisis Staff Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, so I'm a bit perplexed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either it is for the whole region of Krajina or Kljuc. Have you ever seen the document and have you considered it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I've seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03022 receives number D422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P422 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to call 65 ter, Prosecution number 06604.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can see the conclusions which were adopted at the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina nine days after those from the previous document. This meeting was held on the 29th of May, 1992. That's the date when these conclusions were adopted. And under item 1, it reads -- we need "Conclusions." It's at the end of the page in the B/C/S version and on the following page in the English version. An exchange of population is discussed there. And it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see another page in English. Yeah, now we have "Conclusions," under 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads: "It has been decided that all Muslims and Croats, who so wish, should be able to move out of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina ..." And once again we see the same that we saw a little while ago: "But on condition that Serbs living outside the Serbian Autonomous Districts and regions are also allowed to move into the territories of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In this manner, an exchange of population, or, more precisely, a resettlement of people from one part of the former SRBiH to another would be carried out in an organised manner."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could show the following page in B/C/S, please. [In English] I cannot see it in English. We have to go back in English version. One page back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What text are you looking for, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Crisis Staff also decided to decisively oppose any attempt of moving out the population by force or under any kind of pressure and to prevent any such attempts by all available legal means." [In English] So I don't see that sentence in English version. We'll have to compare it. But I see it in B/C/S version. It's second paragraph on the page on our screens in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any chance that the English contains two documents and that you are looking at the second paragraph on page 3, which is the second English document under this same 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I believe you, Your Honour, if you saw it [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at page 3 in English and then page 1 in the B/C/S. Now, perhaps it's the -- in B/C/S, perhaps I took the wrong page, Mr. Lukic. Was it the second page or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second -- next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But there are two second paragraphs on this page. One on the top, there we have two, three, four five.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, second paragraph without number. It says [B/C/S spoken], second paragraph without number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's page 19 from the document. And here, on the English version, I -- under conclusions I see it's marked that it's page 23. There are other conclusions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that in the -- in the B/C/S version, the last item starting at the bottom of page 1 is -- starts with number 23. And that seems to be the same as in the English version, starting on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on page 3 under number 23. If we are looking at the second paragraph, we have to distinguish between numbered paragraphs and non-numbered paragraphs. I think at the bottom of the first page in B/C/S, we find number 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which -- it deals with Muslims and Croats who wish to leave. And that seems to be in the B/C/S also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this item number 1 has three paragraphs and, if I'm not mistaken, you are referring to the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Third one, you are right. Third one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Third one under item 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which then appears on e-court page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that paragraph, I don't see in English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be a -- perhaps a translation error, because in the original, I think, it has four --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- paragraphs. Let's have a look. In English, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It can be the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... one second. After -- we see that the numbering starts with 1 in the B/C/S version five lines on the first page, and then another four and a half lines on the second page. And then we have one long and one short paragraph. Whereas, it seems that in the B/C/S version, we also have a longer and a short paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have to see whether a portion is missing in translation. If so, tell us what is missing and where it is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly the paragraph that I read is missing. The whole paragraph is missing in English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the English version. And could you then please read it again and could the translation, apart from perhaps removing other parts which are not relevant here, could the translation be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I quote: [Interpretation] "At the same time, the Crisis Staff decided to decisively oppose any attempts to move out the population by force or under any kind of pressure and to prevent any such possible attempts by all available legal means."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, obviously you could not have seen this B/C/S portion. But have you used this document at all in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tendered this document into evidence as MFI, because obviously there's something wrong with the translation but we shall see to that and inform the Chamber once it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06604 receives number D423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence -- is marked for identification. I make the same mistake for the second time today. I hope it will not be there for a third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let us look at -- the Prosecution showed you a document during the examination-in-chief, which is now P2877. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that it's a document which is a military secret and not meant to be used by the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it says not to be used by the media, but it's a classified military document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It reads here that "enclosed, we submit the Order" of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, and, actually, we shall look at this enclosed document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would need ... I don't know, page 2. Let's look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see here who were all those it was sent to. Actually, we see it was sent to all the subordinated units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would seem to be the -- the subordinate units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the following page, please. One more page forward, please. We see that the document is dated the 9th of June, 1992. The document comes from the 1st Krajina Corps Command. We'll see that on page 14 in English and page 17 in B/C/S, in the e-court, under (f). We can here that before issuing specific tasks, all soldiers have to be made familiar with the -- the duties that will follow from the corps to a basic unit. And if we could please see the following page, page 15 in English and page 18 in B/C/S under number 11. We can see that the corps requested that each soldier should be familiarised with this. And I quote number 11: "I strictly prohibit any mistreatment of the unarmed civilian population. Treat prisoners of war in accordance with the spirit of the Geneva Conventions." Signed by Commander Major-General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you have come across this document during your work as the Prosecutor showed it to you now, or was it the first time that you saw this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a document I know fairly well, sir. It's referenced in my -- in my report. I'd seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this represents an effort on part of 1st Krajina Corps Command to familiarise all soldiers with the fact that any mistreatment of the civilian population is prohibited?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he -- he is issuing an order. He is making mention that they have to -- they have to abide by these obligations. So in the respect it's an effort. Whether it's the only effort or whether it's enough is a different issue. But, no, he -- he makes -- the document says what it says. He puts that reference in that they should abide by the Geneva Conventions and not mistreat the civilians. And there are others that General Talic sent out, I know, and also referenced in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's see now whether this was implemented or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please look at 1D1451. This is also a document from the 1st Krajina Corps Command from 1993, so the war is already in full swing in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we would need page 2 of the English version in e-court; and, in the B/C/S version, it begins -- as we need item 3 in B/C/S, it begins at the bottom of this page, the part that's marked here and which reads: "The actions of responsible individuals have caused uneasiness among the Muslim population in the villages of Batkovac and Stari Majdan (Sanski Most municipality). Representatives of the ICRC, headed by Mr. Frank, wanted to visit the village of Batkovac but the military officers in charge denied them access." And we would need the following page in B/C/S now, please. The continuation of this paragraph reads: "The 1st Krajina Corps command intervened by sending a military police platoon to protect the population from irresponsible individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you come across this document while preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a document I remember. And it is also dated 1993, March 1993. So my report really focussed on 1992. So I -- it's not a document I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this document demonstrates the continuity of the position held by the 1st Krajina Corps even in 1993, to protect the civilian population of non-Serb ethnicity in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina? We will see more documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it does. I wouldn't -- I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, what does this document show?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows that there -- there is a still remaining small pocket in -- of Muslim -- a Muslim village in Sanski Most in which case there -- the ICRC wanted to visit and that there was some problem with the military there that the corps commander intervened to resolve. I mean, it's the first time I've seen the document. I'd have to read it all. But at face value that's what it is and that's what it seemed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, where do you read that that matter, that is, the access by the ICRC, was resolved? I read that they sent a military police platoon to protect the population from irresponsible individuals. I can't read anything about ICRC then having been given access.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Because you -- your answer suggested that the issue raised was taken care of, whereas I do not read that part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1451 receives number D424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's time -- time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, since we have an extended session, Mr. Lukic, I would like to go on for another five to seven minutes, then take the break, and have then the last session which takes a little bit over one hour as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 03292. It's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by SRNA, the Serbian press agency, which was authorised to publish the following appeal by Radovan Karadzic in connection to the International Red Cross Committee plea. It says under 1: "We ask all the local authorities and the most prominent Serbian individuals to ensure protection and care for all wounded and sick individuals regardless of the side they belong to; to treat all prisoners humanely; to spare the civilians of all attacks; to provide protection and all the possible aid to refugees ..." Did you have this document before you when you compiled your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Mr. Karadzic's positions expressed here, would they have changed anything, in your views?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it would necessarily -- what -- what it would do is put into context some of the other instructions that came out around this time. I think there was decisions taken a couple of days after --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03292 receives number D425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Most of these documents where the witness has no idea, Mr. Lukic, there's no objection by the Prosecution, but, of course, it's not the usual way of introducing documents through a witness. But bar table or -- that's not of primarily importance at this moment for this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you ruled previously, Your Honour, it is crucial for this report to see what is used, what is not used. And it is crucial to see the documents that I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... contradiction of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do not know whether this contradicts the report. I'm hesitant to see it that way. But, as I said before, bar table or through the witness seems not to be the most important issue at this moment, and in the absence of any objections the Chamber has now -- have admitted it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up another document, 1D1454.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an announcement to the citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was signed by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is 11 July 1992. After the session of the assembly which was discussed by you in this courtroom, the Presidency says in this announcement, and I quote: "The Presidency reminds everybody that the Geneva Conventions provide for the relocation of the population from war zones. Likewise, moving out can only be a voluntary act. In keeping with that, it cannot be either prevented or instigated. "To all the citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of Croat and Muslim ethnicities, they are guaranteed all the rights provided for by a state with the rule of law. The authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will not force anybody to stay in the area of combat activities because that would mean that people will become hostages. They will not forcibly move them out because that would constitute ethnic cleansing. All refugees from the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be allowed to return without suffering any consequences; criminals, and not civilians, are subject to legal sanctions." Did you review this document when preparing your analysis? Did you take it into account, if you did?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously this is a document which is in the possession of the Prosecutor's office. It has an ERN number. I believe that the issue was also raised by His Honour Judge Orie. Who was it who decided which documents you were allowed to use as opposed to the document which you were not supposed to use? Who made a short list of the material for you to peruse?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I exploited were the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps, predominantly that collection, and some other documents that I obtained through searches that I did that reflected or had relevance to the 1st Krajina Corps documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So not only did you not study the documentation produced by the enemy side, you also did not study the Serbian documentation that went beyond the scope of the material produced by the 1st Krajina Corps. Would that, more or less, summarise what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did include some materials which were not solely in the 1st Krajina Corps archive. But, as I said to you before, this document and report has got limitations and it does not review every single document. It was not a report about all aspects of the political situation in Bosnia and the RS territory, and there will be documents I did not review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few more question, two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you regard this document as important for your analysis, or would you consider it of no consequence at all?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would -- I would certainly consider it and -- and look at it and -- and put it in its context in terms of time and other aspects that were going on in relation to, say, the Presidency decisions or operations that had already occurred prior to this situation -- that occurred prior to this and what happened after this, whether any of this actually was implemented. So I would -- I would look at this document and I would put it in some -- some context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender the document into evidence. And this, indeed, is the time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 1D1454 receives number D426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D426 is admitted into evidence. The witness may follow the usher. We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber wondered whether you could not have agreed with the Prosecution on the existence of these press statements and then quote in one line to the witness and ask him whether that would change his views on the matter. I mean, unless there's any dispute about these press releases or statements being made. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, in these cases, there hasn't been, Mr. President. Obviously I'm not sure what else Mr. Lukic would choose to use but we're always open to coming to such agreements with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we couldn't speed up considerably. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at a new document, 1D1455. This also goes against your claim that people kept on leaving all the time and forever. This is an instruction which was sent to all presidents of municipalities. It says in here -- unfortunately, I could not read the B/C/S version. I'm going to quote from the English version because the B/C/S version seems to be rather illegible: [In English] "The occurrence of abandoned flats is a war issue and so are the refugees. This means that both occurrences are temporary."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you come across this document in your work?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I didn't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on all the documents that were shown to you, would you consider changing your positions stated in paragraphs 2.138 and 2.149?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- no, I wouldn't, sir. I -- going back to this particular document, it is not clear whether the reference here is to do with individuals who have fled or whether it's to do with Serb refugees who have come into RS territory and are taking -- are taking flats or accommodation. So, no, I wouldn't change ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tendered the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1455 receives number D427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D427 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at a military document, 65 ter 02649. It's a Prosecution number. It was issued by the command of a group of brigades in Skender Vakuf. It was issued on the 6th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was before the international journalists visited the area; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's certainly before and Gutman and Penny Marshall and those visits in late July. I don't know whether other visits may have occurred from other journalists in between, but certainly from those journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document we are looking at English 3 and page 7 in B/C/S. There are a few empty pages in the B/C/S version of the document between the typed up pages; hence, the discrepancy in pagination. In the English version, I don't seem to be able to find the exact line. The line should start with the following word, "Use some of the forces ..." and I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 5.2. Number 5.2, paragraph 3, but it is hardly visible. It's ... line [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

Page 16 [In English] page 13 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not what it says in 2.138. It says, "Indicate an articulation of the plan to remove down to the lowest levels." This document is what it says. Colonel Peulic has put that in his instructions, but I don't think it necessarily is really related to 2.138.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Or do you perhaps think and suggest that this document that is on the screen is exactly in line with your views?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document on the screen is a different issue. This is a combat instruction that Colonel Peulic is passing down to the units of his Operational Group. And within that, he is tasking his brigades to take -- take control of territory, including, Kotor Varos, Skender Vakuf and other areas. And with -- and with -- and within that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have no time for these long explanations. I'm not interested. I want to be told whether this is in agreement with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. The witness may finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I need the next week for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber will decide how much time you'll get. The witness may finish this answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be brief, it's an instruction to take control of the territory in his zone, and within that, yes, he does make mention that civilians are not to be mistreated. But it's not -- it doesn't make reference of resettlement. It's about combat operations his brigades are going to undertake at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, according to you, the fact that mistreatment of the civilian population is prohibited does not have an impact on the resettlement of the self-same civilian population and that this is a plan of some kind.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see there's different issues. One is this is a military --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You've told me "no." Thank you. We move on. In paragraph 2. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic please repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.141. In English version, it's page 113, and in B/C/S, page 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this process of exchange, was there anything in the activities of the Croats and the Muslims that was unlawful?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the document, sir, on the screen? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The paragraph of your report, 2.141. You say from the writing of the 30th Division it's obvious that the Muslims and the Croats who requested leave to move were actually resettled and that the exchanges of civilians were agreed between the Serbs and the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anything unlawful about the activities of non-Serbs in these exchanges, so the non-Serbs who take part in negotiations with the Serb side and exchange Serbs for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say, sir, because I'm not sure of the negotiations and agreements. If your underlying question relates to whether Serbs, say in Jajce, in relation here were under pressure to move out or were moved out, it would not surprise me if that was not the case. I can't say for sure because I don't know the details on the other side. It's clear from this document there is this resettlement issue that ethnic groups are being moved in and out from Jajce. Whether that's legal, illegal, whether it's pressure on both side, whether it's forced on both sides, it's not clear from the document. I'm using the document to say there were examples of this type of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we'll focus on paragraph 2.152 of your report. In English version, it's page 116 and in B/C/S, page 119. You saw there that unlawfully property -- mainly immovable property was appropriated, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic please repeat. He is reading very fast a text we do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to repeat your reading because the interpreters were not able to follow it at your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you claim in this paragraph that in an organised manner the ownership of immovable property was organised, mainly land and apartments. Do you know who were the owners of apartments in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time? And are you familiar with the concept of tenants' rights?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Property ownership wasn't really an area of my study, sir. But I am aware of, more generally I guess, the -- I suspect the issue of tenants' rights and that individuals can be tenants in property that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that someone who does not have property cannot lose it? And are you aware of the obligation to return apartments always when someone is moving from one place to another in the Former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, if someone moved from one place to another, he had to return the apartment to its owner, perhaps a company, or a municipality, or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, property ownership is not really an area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question, were you aware, sir, Mr. Brown, that -- which ethnicity had occupied, not owned, occupied these apartments that Mr. Lukic is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, it would seem from the document these are non-Serbs who are -- who are leaving this -- this accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then occupation is a right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine. Well, yes, occupation is a right. You don't -- even in my own country if you don't own your property but are a tenant in it there are strict legal rights that you have. You cannot be turfed out your house on an afternoon and told you are no longer welcome there. There are legal rights, legal processes by which if someone wants to reclaim that property or move you from it, that they can do so but you have certain rights to remain there until that is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And since I'm going to move to another document, I would ask for this one to be admitted, 65 ter 2649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02649 receives number D428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D428 is admitted into evidence. Before we move to another area, Mr. Lukic -- and, Witness, can I ask you, in paragraph 2.152 did you express yourself on the details of what could be legally done, or are you first distinguishing between organised, authorised, whatever you name it, transfer of occupancy other than the non-organised of the -- what you call "illegal," in brackets, and the involvement of the 1st Krajina Corps in those movements? Is that what you were talking about or were you giving in judgement on what was legal or illegal in respect of those abandoned apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not making a call on the property and legal issues, per se. What I wanted to do was when I reviewed certain documents, it seemed to be that on the one hand there were references by General Talic that he was unhappy with -- individuals occupying territory -- property of their own back. And that -- that he didn't approve of that but that he was approving of the official, i.e., Bosnian Serb, policy, that these apartments or properties should be put at the control of the RS authorities and dealt with -- and handed out in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In footnote 561, you refer to a document in order to support this claim of yours that the army probably didn't criticise this officially agreement distribution of property because it profited from it because you say that soldiers moved into those apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I just ask that if he's -- that if Mr. Lukic is quoting or purporting to quote the proposition for which the witness has cited the document, he be reasonably precise about it. I don't see, for instance, in that paragraph a refreshes to the army criticising this policy or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 559, the footnote number in paragraph 2.152, you say that: "The army probably did not criticise such officially authorised seizing and distribution of property because it profited from it."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you originally referred us to footnote 561. That's what we are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we can look into the same document in relation of this claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document from that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't confuse us, Mr. Lukic. If you look at paragraph 78, line 2, you say in footnote 561 you refer to, so we are looking at footnote 561. Now when you change and say after 559, the footnote number, 55 -- after 559 is 560.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a text after 559. That's what I was -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we need document 65 ter, Prosecution number, 02968.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, we see before us a report about abandoned apartments. Do you know -- or, rather, do you accept - I will tell you - that the underlined words are actually the names of the apartment owners or the companies, the municipality, the medical centre, the secretariat of the interior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which underlined word, Mr. Lukic? I see no underlined word in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, on the first page you have "DP Proleter." It means "state company, Proleter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The question to the witness is whether the witness agrees that these headings refer to social institutions or companies which owned the apartments referred to. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether these are names of companies or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise Serbian names on these lists? That is to say, are there any apartments here that were abandoned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't necessarily tell you and I wouldn't really want to -- to delve into -- I can recognise some names as being, say, Muslim. I -- I can't necessarily tell you whether other names are -- are Serb or not. It's not really my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you tell us in a little bit more about the document. There's no time on it, who drafted it, where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can tell us more. I cannot. It's footnoted in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any idea? Where is it footnoted, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in 561, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was a -- Kotor Varos War Presidency, part of that collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Obviously I haven't had time to do a comprehensive review of our records but what the witness has said is consistent with the information that I'm finding [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there any time-frame to be given to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Our records reflect that it's part of a collection of files and records from 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we -- is this -- the names appearing on this list, are those the names of person who now occupy those apartments, or those who had abandoned them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the names on the left-hand side were the former owners, and the -- who had abandoned the property or left. And the names down the right-hand side are individuals who've taken over those properties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now see it. So that currently inhabited by gives the new occupant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you can recognise some names. Would you agree that names under numbers 2, 3, 12, 16, 18, and 21 only in this first group of apartments noted as property of the socially owned enterprise Proleter are names of Serbs whose apartments were included on this list?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to defer to you, sir, or others. It's not really something I would feel comfortable in saying. But I would defer to you that maybe there are Serb names here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that they were recorded -- all the flats that had been abandoned were recorded and managed by their owners, i.e., the companies who owned them?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I really am not sure that I can answer that, sir. As I say, I'm not an expert on this issue of property ownership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since the footnote, 561, refers especially to Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic, I would like to see that name in the document. Perhaps we can go to the next page in English. It's a reference only to this person, Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic. Can we go to the next page. I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe it will be page 3 in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry. I believe it will be page 3 in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3. Now it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kotor Varos, under number 9, I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would bring us to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02968 receives number D429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. One question, Mr. Lukic. You suggested that the property was still administered by the owners. First of all, I see now and then illegally, which apparently means that the owner is not administering. But, second, I don't see that it is administered by the owners. I see, for example, for Novakovic that he inhabits the apartment by the order of the War Presidency. Now you could consider municipal assembly perhaps in the same area, but where does it say that apart from being the owner of the apartment building or apartment block that they play a role in -- in -- in managing them? I do not see it yet, but if you would assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are many ways of managing in socialist times with a building like [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine but [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously -- obviously from this document I can accept that it's done by War Presidency who distributed the apartments. I don't have [Overlapping speakers] ... there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't know. You suggested that the owners still managed their property. Now in your explanation, you are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Property has to be returned to the owner and they manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The simple answer, therefore, is that it gives information who inhabits at this moment or who [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... or who left the apartment because there is many empty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- still empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But who manages it? The document does not provide any information for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right. I cannot see that from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] And now let's look at 65 ter 03084, another Prosecutor's document. The document will be related to Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says in the document that the War Presidency adopts the following decision on criteria required in order for people to move out of Kljuc municipality. The document was issued on the 30th of July, 1992, or, rather, it refers to that date. In this decision, under 2, you can see how people can move out of Kljuc municipality forever, permanently. Article 2: "Persons who have exchanged their real estate (privately-owned houses, land and flats) with other individuals from the area to which they are moving shall be permitted to leave the municipality permanently." Did you know that that was a condition which people had to meet if they wanted to move out permanently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just object to the characterisation of the condition. I think there's an alternative condition two lines below, and so I think the document is being slightly misstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness to read Article 2, if he's able to do. And then put any question to the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. However, we can look at the document together and we can combine the two questions. Instead of exchanging one's property, people could actually leave it to Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document is what it is. It does have those two -- those two options. In essence, if you don't meet the time deadline, the municipality will do it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, isn't the -- one of the real issues in Article 2, the option which does not appear, that is, leave as you wish and come back and enjoy your property again, which you own; but that it's -- if you want to leave for a shorter or a longer period of time, you can't keep the ownership of your property. Is -- isn't that the -- one of the issue that appears rather than to say, Well, there are two different options of getting rid of your property but keeping your property. Is that the really issue? And perhaps the witness could comment on it, or if you have any further questions on what seems to me to be similarly an issue with Article 2. Could you comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, sometimes it's what's not in the documents that are as powerful as what's in it, and this is a clear example. You know, if -- if this was an issue of, We have a conflict in Kljuc which some of you may feel frightened enough to leave, but don't worry your property will be okay to come back to, there should be an echo of that, that you are within your rights to come back when you feel safe to do so. But here it seems to be that if you leave it for a period of time that Kljuc is going to decide what is going to happen to your property. There is also the issue at this time that a large number of people in Kljuc were already in detention camps and whether they had any ability or chance or opportunity to deal with property matters whilst they were being held in these detention camps, I would very much doubt. So there is more to it than just this seeming anodyne or bureaucratic issue of property passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the last paragraph of Article 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- it's a -- I -- it -- for what reason are you not allowed to sell your property other than -- I think that they -- it's -- it's an odd comment to put in. People are -- if you -- I mean, paragraph -- Article 2 is talking about privately-owned property. It's yours. You can presumably sell it to whoever you want. But here there is a -- there is -- they are citizens that right. What they're allowing is this issue of exchange under strict conditions and it strikes me that this again cuts to this issue of -- you know, these people are going to be moving out. We will -- when you -- when you read some of the delegates at the 16th Assembly Session who are talking about this very issue of, What are we going to do with Serbs who are in areas who we don't control? Well, we need to have this exchange. We need to move this -- these -- these types of minutiae seem to echo that ultimately these individuals weren't going to come back, no matter what the public facade was. And I actually think the practical reality is that these people didn't come back and certainly the ones in the camp never had any chance to come back at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this ban on the sale of property that you find confusing was actually introduced in order to prevent any possible abuses. For example, a person might be forced at gunpoint to sell their property and that would be the purpose of this decision, which I suggest to you. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think then we must make a distinction because you're making an assumption which doesn't appear from the document. And the document then should prohibit forced sales, not just sales. You can laugh, but if it's at gunpoint it's a forced sale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you have to prove because before this moment, Your Honour, many forgeries, actually forced transfers were made and then citizens would have to prove that it was forced or not forced sale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are testifying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am because I took part in many returns of these flats, so I know it perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's wait for you to call a witness to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the point is, faced with this document, there's no reference to forced sale or voluntarily sale. It just says sale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any sale. Any sale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any sale, so therefore -- therefore, it becomes arbitrary to deny a person the right to sell voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Trust me, it's in the best interests of population [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I don't know. We'll find out when you call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you put your next question to the witness. But I would have one observation, Mr. Lukic.
